short: The unit models read and write; roughly three-quarters of an English word. Pricing and context limits are counted in tokens.
long: A token is a chunk of text produced by the model's tokenizer: common words are one token, rare words or code split into several. A million tokens is about 750,000 words of English. Different models tokenise the same text into different counts, so compare cost per task rather than per token.

short: The maximum text a model can consider in one request: prompt, documents, conversation and answer combined.
long: Measured in tokens. Flagship models in 2026 advertise around one million tokens. Everything in the window is billed as input on each request, and accuracy on very long inputs is lower than on short ones.

short: A neural network trained on vast amounts of text to predict the next token, which turns out to be enough to write, summarise, reason and code.
long: LLMs are the engines behind ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini. They are trained in two stages: pre-training on general text, then post-training (instruction tuning and reinforcement learning) to make them helpful and safe.

short: An AI system that pursues a goal by taking actions with tools, in a loop, rather than answering a single question.
long: See the explainer [What is an AI agent?](/learn/what-is-an-ai-agent/). The risk and value of an agent both come from the tools and permissions it has.

short: The text sent to a model: instructions, context and the question.
long: Prompts usually have a system part (standing instructions from the developer) and a user part. Prompt design strongly affects output quality and cost.

short: Standing instructions a developer gives a model that apply to every conversation, such as persona, rules and output format.
long: System prompts are a prime candidate for prompt caching because they repeat across requests.

short: An attack in which text the model reads, such as a web page or email, contains instructions that hijack its behaviour.
long: See [Prompt injection explained](/learn/prompt-injection-explained/). The main security concern for agents.

short: A user's attempt to make a model ignore its safety rules through crafted prompts.
long: Distinct from prompt injection, which is carried out by a third party through content the model processes.

short: A confident, fluent model output that is false or unsupported.
long: Reduced by grounding (RAG), by instructing the model to cite sources and say when it does not know, and by verification steps. Not eliminated by any current model.

short: Finding the relevant passages from a document store and giving them to the model with the question, so answers are grounded in your data.
long: See [RAG explained for business leaders](/learn/rag-explained-for-business/).

short: A list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of text, so similar texts have similar numbers.
long: Embeddings power semantic search and RAG: documents and questions are embedded, and the nearest documents to the question are retrieved.

short: A database optimised for storing embeddings and finding the nearest ones to a query.
long: Used as the retrieval layer in RAG systems. Many conventional databases now offer vector search.

short: Further training a model on your own examples to change its behaviour or specialise it.
long: Useful for consistent style, narrow tasks and reducing prompt length. Compared with RAG it is slower to update and harder to audit, and does not reliably teach new facts.

short: Running a trained model to produce output. What you pay for when you call an API.
long: Inference cost scales with tokens processed and model size, which is why smaller tiers and shorter outputs are cheaper.

short: The process of adjusting a model's parameters on data. Pre-training builds general ability; post-training shapes behaviour.
long: Frontier training runs cost hundreds of millions to billions of dollars in compute, which is why only a handful of labs train top-tier models.

short: The numbers inside a model that training adjusts; loosely, its size. Frontier models have hundreds of billions to trillions.
long: More parameters generally means more capability and higher inference cost, though training data and technique matter as much.

short: Another word for a model's parameters, usually in the context of publishing or downloading them.
long: See [open-weight vs closed models](/learn/open-weights-vs-closed-models/).

short: A model whose trained parameters are published for anyone to download and run.
long: Not the same as open source: training data and code are usually not released. Examples include Llama, Mistral's open releases, Gemma and DeepSeek.

short: A model reachable only through its vendor's API; the weights are not published.
long: GPT-6 Astra, Claude Fable and Gemini are closed. Advantages: capability, features, no operations. Disadvantages: data leaves your environment and the vendor controls availability.

short: The neural network architecture behind nearly all current language models, built around a mechanism called attention.
long: Introduced in 2017. Its ability to process sequences in parallel made training on internet-scale text practical.

short: The mechanism that lets a transformer weigh which earlier tokens matter when producing the next one.
long: Attention cost grows with sequence length, which is why very long context windows are expensive and were slow to arrive.

short: A model trained to work through a problem step by step, generating intermediate 'thinking' tokens, before answering.
long: Reasoning models score higher on maths, code and planning at the cost of more output tokens and latency. Many vendors expose a reasoning budget or effort setting.

short: A setting that controls how many thinking tokens a reasoning model may use before answering.
long: Higher budgets raise accuracy on hard tasks and cost. Benchmark scores often quote the maximum setting.

short: Charging a reduced rate for the repeated prefix of a prompt, such as a system prompt or a document reused across requests.
long: Cache reads cost 2.5% to 10% of the input price at the major vendors. Put stable content first in the prompt to benefit.

short: A way to submit many requests to be processed asynchronously, usually within hours, at about half price.
long: Offered by OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. Ideal for backfills, evaluations and nightly jobs.

short: A model that accepts or produces more than one kind of input or output: text, images, audio, video.
long: Most flagship models now read images; audio and video are billed at different token rates.

short: A standard test used to compare models, such as a set of coding tasks or exam questions.
long: See [How to read an AI benchmark](/learn/how-to-read-an-ai-benchmark/). Vendor-run results are claims; independent runs are evidence.

short: A test set with known-good answers used to measure a model or system on your own tasks.
long: The single most useful artefact an AI team can build. Fifty to two hundred real examples is enough to start.

short: Checks placed around a model to block unwanted inputs or outputs, such as filters for sensitive data or policy violations.
long: Guardrails reduce risk but can be bypassed; they complement, rather than replace, careful permissioning of what the system can do.

short: The broad effort to make models behave as their developers and users intend, including being honest and refusing harmful requests.
long: Covers training techniques (such as reinforcement learning from human feedback), evaluations and deployment policies.

short: Reinforcement learning from human feedback: training a model to prefer outputs that human raters rate highly.
long: The post-training technique that turned raw language models into usable assistants. Successors use AI feedback and verifiable rewards.

short: A model's ability to request that the surrounding software run a function, such as a search or a database query, and return the result.
long: The building block of agents. The model does not execute anything itself; the application does, which is where permissions must be enforced.

short: An open standard for connecting AI applications to tools and data sources through a common interface.
long: Lets a tool be written once and used by many AI clients. Security reviews should treat each MCP server as an integration with the permissions it is granted.

short: How long a model takes to respond, usually measured as time to first token and tokens per second.
long: Smaller tiers and shorter outputs are faster. Reasoning budgets and long contexts add latency.

short: The maximum requests or tokens per minute a vendor allows an account, often tiered by spending history.
long: A common cause of production failures. Design for retries and consider batch for non-urgent work.

short: Application programming interface: the way software calls a model, billed per token, as opposed to a chat app used by a person.
long: ChatGPT Plus and Claude Pro are subscriptions for people; the API is what developers build on.

short: Training a smaller model to imitate a larger one's outputs, capturing much of its capability at lower cost.
long: How vendors produce mini, Flash and Haiku tiers, and a point of dispute in vendor terms of service.

short: A model design where only a subset of parameters activates for each token, giving large capacity at lower inference cost.
long: Common in frontier and open-weight models. A 'total parameters' figure for an MoE model overstates its per-token compute.

short: Training data generated by a model rather than collected from humans.
long: Used to fill gaps in real data and to train reasoning. Risks include amplifying the generating model's errors.

short: A model at or near the state of the art at the time, typically the newest top tier from a major lab.
long: Frontier models are the subject of most safety policies and regulations, which often set capability or compute thresholds.

short: The processing power, usually GPU or TPU hours, used to train and run models. The scarce input of the AI industry.
long: Data-center capacity, power and chip export controls are compute stories. Most AI infrastructure news is about who can get compute and at what price.

short: Graphics processing unit: the chip type, dominated by Nvidia, that performs the parallel arithmetic AI training and inference require.
long: GPU supply, pricing and export rules shape which labs and countries can build frontier models.

short: A credential used by software, including AI agents, rather than a person, such as a service account or API key.
long: Agents multiply non-human identities. Securing their permissions and rotation is an emerging category of security tooling.

short: Synthetic audio, image or video that convincingly impersonates a real person.
long: A fraud and misinformation risk; detection tools exist but lag generation. Verify unusual requests through a second channel.

short: Supplying a model with trusted sources (documents, search results) so its answer is tied to evidence rather than memory.
long: RAG is one form of grounding; search-augmented answering is another. Grounded answers can cite sources.

short: In a mixture-of-experts model, the subset of parameters actually used for each token. Inkling 2 Small has 594B total but about 17B active.
long: Sparse models route each token to a few of many expert sub-networks, so only a fraction of the weights do work on any given token. Total parameters set memory requirements and, loosely, knowledge capacity; active parameters set per-token compute, latency and serving cost. Comparing models by total parameters alone is misleading when one is sparse and the other dense.

short: The software around a model that turns it into an agent: tool connections, memory, permissions, retries and the loop that decides what to do next.
long: The model supplies judgement; the harness supplies everything else. Open-source harnesses such as DeepSeek Harness, and vendor ones such as Claude Code or Codex, handle tool calling, context management, permission prompts and plugins. Most agent security properties live in the harness rather than the model, which is why a harness default such as saving approved commands to a file can leak secrets regardless of which model is running.

short: Automated detection of credentials (API keys, passwords, tokens) in code, configuration and history before or after they are committed.
long: Scanners such as Gitleaks and TruffleHog match known key formats and high-entropy strings in repositories, pull requests and CI pipelines. They miss credentials that do not look like keys, for example a password typed inside a shell command, which is why agent configuration files need dedicated rules. Effective programmes scan git history as well as the current tree and rotate anything found rather than just deleting it.

short: The FDA pathway that lets a device, including AI software, reach market by showing it is substantially equivalent to an already-authorised predicate device.
long: Most of the more than a thousand AI-enabled medical devices FDA has authorised went through 510(k) rather than the more demanding de novo or premarket approval routes. The pathway works when the intended use is narrow and a comparable predicate exists; it fits poorly with models that update frequently or systems with broad clinical roles, which is what predetermined change-control plans and proposals such as the PATIENT AI Act try to address.

short: Publishing a model's weights only after a sequence of gated steps, typically API access, external safety testing and red-teaming, rather than on launch day.
long: Because open weights cannot be withdrawn once downloaded, some labs now treat publication as the last step rather than the first. Thinking Machines' framework, used for Inkling 2 Small, makes each stage conditional on evidence from the previous one. Critics note it delays independent evaluation; supporters argue it is the only way to combine open weights with a credible safety process.

short: The two phases of inference: reading the whole prompt in one parallel pass (prefill), then generating the answer one token at a time (decode).
long: Prefill is fast per token because every input token can be processed at once; decode is sequential and memory-bound, which is why output tokens cost roughly five times input tokens on every major price list. Serving systems batch many users' decode steps together to keep accelerators busy.

short: Hardware that keeps data and model weights encrypted and isolated while they are being processed, not only at rest or in transit.
long: Confidential computing uses trusted execution environments in the CPU or accelerator so that even the cloud operator cannot read what is being computed. Google's TPU 8tx, paired with AMD EPYC hosts, brings this to TPU fine-tuning and inference; Nvidia offers it on its H100 and later GPUs. It matters for regulated data and for protecting proprietary weights on shared infrastructure.

short: A robot foundation model that predicts how the world will change and chooses actions from that prediction, rather than mapping images straight to motor commands.
long: Where a vision-language-action model outputs actions directly from what it sees and is told, a world action model first simulates the likely outcome of candidate actions using a learned world model, then acts. Nvidia's GR00T 2, built on its Cosmos world models, is the most prominent example; the approach is more compute-intensive per step but can generalise better to new tasks from human video.

short: Stealing API keys or cloud credentials to run large language models at someone else's expense, or to resell that access.
long: The term covers a growing criminal market in stolen model-API credentials, which can be used for compute, for jailbroken services, or sold on. Inference and fine-tuning platforms are attractive targets because they store customers' credentials for other services as job secrets. The defence is short-lived scoped keys, spend alerts and rotation that happens at the issuing provider, since deleting a stored copy of a key does not revoke it.

short: What it costs to get a job completed by a model, including hidden reasoning tokens, retries and tool calls, as opposed to the list price per token.
long: Independent evaluators such as Artificial Analysis now publish cost per task alongside benchmark scores because models with identical token prices can differ threefold in what they cost to finish the same work. A model that emits fewer output tokens, or declines rather than guesses, is cheaper per task even at the same list price. Budget forecasts built on token prices alone systematically underestimate agent workloads.

short: Mathematically proving that software or hardware satisfies a precise specification, usually with a proof assistant such as Lean that checks every step.
long: Unlike testing, which shows the presence of bugs on the inputs tried, formal verification shows their absence for every input covered by the specification. It has been reserved for kernels, compilers and avionics because writing the proofs cost person-years; in November 2026 DeepMind's AlphaProof Code generated about 6.5 million lines of Lean proof for Signal's protocol code in four weeks. The result is only as good as the specification, which remains human-reviewed.

short: A vendor's own vendor that handles your data on its behalf, such as the inference provider behind a SaaS product's AI feature.
long: Data-protection law requires vendors to list sub-processors and flow contractual obligations down to them. AI features have added a layer most registers miss: the hosted model provider, and sometimes that provider's cloud host. The Fireworks AI breach reached Notion customers through exactly this chain. Ask every vendor with an AI feature which models it runs, where, and under what retention.

short: The window after an IPO during which insiders and pre-IPO investors are barred from selling shares, typically 180 days.
long: Lock-ups prevent a flood of insider selling in the first months of trading. Anthropic's filing restricts most holders for 180 days and founders and large holders for up to 365, with some early release if price conditions are met after an earnings report. Lock-up expiries are among the biggest scheduled events for a newly listed stock with a small free float.

short: Software that simulates rigid bodies, contact and friction so robot control policies can be trained on millions of virtual trials before touching hardware.
long: Engines such as Nvidia's PhysX, DeepMind's MuJoCo and the open-source Newton run thousands of parallel environments on a GPU. Throughput, measured in environment steps per second, sets the cost of training; Skild AI's Steel solver claims a 3.8x average gain over PhysX. Speed only matters if policies trained in simulation transfer to real robots, the sim-to-real problem.

short: A model that scores a fixed set of options and returns probabilities instead of generating text, used for routing, tool selection, policy checks and grading.
long: Google's Gemini Decision 1 and OpenAI's Decisions API both run in a single forward pass with no decode loop, so they answer in 150–250 ms and are billed on input tokens only. They cannot explain themselves or notice that none of the options fit, so generative fallback is still needed for open-ended cases.

short: A hard monthly or daily limit on what an API key can charge, set at the provider, after which requests fail.
long: The cheapest control against LLMjacking: a stolen key with a cap loses a bounded amount. Pair it with a model and region allow-list, because a cap limits the bill, not what the key can reach. Railway's October breach ran up about $740,000 across customer keys that mostly had neither.

short: The published safety policy a large frontier developer must maintain under New York's RAISE Act and California's SB 53, describing how it assesses and mitigates catastrophic risk.
long: RAISE requires the framework to be reviewed at least annually, material changes published within 30 days, a transparency report with each new model, critical incidents reported within 72 hours and quarterly confidential summaries of internal risk assessments. Only companies above $500 million in revenue training models above 10^26 FLOPs are covered.

short: A company's operating loss after excluding items it chooses to leave out, typically stock compensation and one-off charges; not a GAAP measure.
long: OpenAI's reported $10.9 billion third-quarter figure is adjusted and comes from internal documents, while Anthropic's $567 million operating loss is from an audited S-1. The two are not directly comparable; always check what 'adjusted' removes before quoting a margin.

short: Breaking out of the isolation that is supposed to keep one tenant's code, or one agent's actions, from reaching the host or other tenants.
long: Railway's October breach began with a partial filesystem-isolation escape on a shared build VM that exposed a build credential. The same class of flaw matters for AI agents that execute code: an agent sandbox is only as strong as the boundary and the credentials visible inside it. Per-task ephemeral VMs with narrowly scoped credentials are the standard fix.

short: Nvidia's 4-bit floating-point weight format, used to train and serve very large models on Blackwell-class GPUs with roughly a quarter of the memory of 16-bit weights.
long: Inkling 2 Small was trained natively in NVFP4 and shipped that way: 594 billion parameters in about 394 GB. The catch is hardware: NVFP4 kernels target Blackwell (B200, B300, GB300) and need conversion or special kernels on older or non-Nvidia accelerators, which is why 'open weights' and 'runnable on your cluster' are not the same thing.

short: Splitting a mixture-of-experts model across GPUs by expert rather than by layer, so each GPU holds a subset of the experts and tokens are routed to the right device.
long: Large MoE models such as Inkling 2 Small (8 of 384 experts active per token) are served with expert parallelism, often combined with tensor parallelism. Some model cards require the two degrees to be equal, which constrains which GPU counts and topologies work. If a serving framework has not merged support for a model's parallelism scheme, the weights are downloadable but not yet deployable.

short: A vendor setting that controls how much reasoning a model does before answering, trading latency and tokens for accuracy; Google's Gemini 4 models offer low, medium, high and xhigh.
long: The same model can score very differently at different thinking levels, and cost very differently too, because reasoning tokens are billed as output. Gemini 4 Hydrogen reports an Artificial Analysis index of 51 at high and 54 at xhigh. When comparing vendors' benchmark claims, check which level was used; when comparing bills, measure tokens per task at the level you actually run.

short: A tort claim that conduct harms the public's health, safety or shared rights; historically used against pollution and opioids, now pleaded against frontier AI development.
long: The November 2026 suit by Public Citizen and others asks a San Francisco court to bar five labs from building more capable models on public-nuisance grounds, citing the labs' own risk warnings as evidence. Such claims rarely produce injunctions against an industry, but they open discovery into internal safety evaluations, which is the practical risk for defendants.

short: A small script an attacker uploads to a web server so they can run commands on it through a browser; the classic first foothold in a server intrusion.
long: In the AntiFox intrusions documented by Arctic Wolf, an AI pentest agent dropped an ASPX webshell on an IIS server and used it to read configuration files containing AWS keys. Detection is file-based (new scripts in web directories) and behavioural (a web process spawning shells). Correlating a new webshell with a burst of cloud API calls is now the signature of an agent-driven attack.
